title: Plato's Utopia
orientation: This chapter examines the political core of Plato's Republic: the earliest Utopia in Western literature. Russell walks through Plato's ideal city -- its three classes, its censored education, its communism of property and of family, and its 'noble lie' -- before turning to Plato's definition of 'justice' and using it to launch a broader philosophical debate about whether ethical claims can be objectively true at all. The chapter matters because nearly every subsequent utopian and totalitarian political scheme echoes some feature of this founding text.
historical_background: The Republic was written against the background Russell has already supplied: Sparta's real and mythical example, Plato's aristocratic upbringing, Athens's defeat in the Peloponnesian War, and the execution of Socrates. Russell notes that, unlike modern Utopias written as pure literary exercises, Plato's Republic may have been meant to be actually founded -- many of its provisions were already realized, in some form, at Sparta, and philosopher-rule had been attempted by Pythagoras and, in Plato's own day, by Archytas at Taras.
philosophical_problems: What is 'justice,' and can a definition of justice in the state be transferred to justice in the individual?
How should a state organize education, property, and family to produce a stable, virtuous ruling class?
Is government by an unelected, specially trained elite ('guardians') compatible with justice?
Is there an objective standard of 'good' and 'bad,' or are ethical disputes ultimately contests of power?

philosophers_discussed.name: Plato
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Primary subject: Russell reconstructs, in detail, the ideal city set out in the Republic (through Book V and the definition of justice in Book IV), including its class structure, education, eugenics, communism, and 'noble lie,' and subjects Plato's definition of justice to sustained criticism.

philosophers_discussed.name: Thrasymachus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A Sophist from Chalcedon who appears in Book I of the Republic and bluntly asserts that 'justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger'; Russell argues Socrates never fairly answers this challenge, which raises the deep question of whether ethical claims can be objectively true.

philosophers_discussed.name: Anaximander
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Quoted briefly to show that Plato's conception of justice as everyone keeping to 'his appointed place and appointed function' descends from an older, pre-philosophical Greek idea of cosmic justice and reparation for transgressing fixed bounds.

core_concepts.name: The three-class Utopia (guardians, soldiers, producers)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Plato divides his ideal city into ordinary workers, soldiers (auxiliaries), and a small ruling class of 'guardians' who alone hold political power, with movement between classes possible only in exceptional cases.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Plato's tripartite social structure in which political authority is restricted to a numerically small guardian class (chosen initially by the legislator, thereafter mainly hereditary, with exceptional promotion or demotion based on merit), a larger soldier class enforcing the guardians' will, and the mass of common people engaged in productive labor.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is the structural backbone of the entire Utopia: nearly every other institution Russell discusses (education, property, family, the noble lie) exists to keep this class structure stable and to ensure the guardians govern as intended.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Modeled partly on Spartan social structure (citizens vs. helots vs. perioeci), discussed in the previous chapter.
examples: Russell compares the guardians to 'the Jesuits in old Paraguay, the ecclesiastics in the States of the Church until 1870, and the Communist Party in the U.S.S.R.'
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: The template of a specially trained, ideologically committed governing minority recurs across later utopian and revolutionary political theory.

core_concepts.name: Censorship of poetry, drama, and music
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Plato bans large parts of Homer and Hesiod, forbids most drama, and restricts which musical modes and rhythms children may hear, all in order to shape virtuous, courageous, and obedient citizens from an early age.
core_concepts.precise_definition: A state-controlled censorship regime covering literature ('music' in the broad sense) presented to the young, justified on the grounds that stories depicting misbehaving gods, expressions of fear of death, excessive laughter, or indulgence in feasting and lust would corrupt future guardians, and that dramatic imitation of villains, women, or inferiors would degrade actors and audiences of good birth.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It shows the illiberal cost, in Russell's reading, of subordinating culture entirely to a predetermined civic and military purpose, and it directly inspired later real-world censorship regimes invoking similar justifications.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Modeled partly on actual Spartan restriction of harmonies to the Dorian and Phrygian modes.
examples: Only the Dorian (courage) and Phrygian (temperance) musical modes are allowed; the Lydian (sorrow) and Ionian (relaxation) are banned.
All dramatists are to be ceremonially honored and then banished from the city, since a good man should not imitate villains, women, or inferiors.
objections: Russell notes the impossibility Plato himself half-recognizes: plays without any flawed characters are not really possible, which is precisely why Plato ends up banishing dramatists altogether rather than reforming drama.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Plato insists the young be taught that 'evils never come from the gods,' reshaping traditional religious stories to serve civic education.

core_concepts.name: Communism of property and of the family
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Guardians are to own no private property beyond bare necessities, and are to have no private families: spouses and children are shared in common, with marriages secretly arranged by lottery-manipulating rulers for eugenic purposes, and children raised without knowing their biological parents.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Plato's proposal that the guardian (and possibly soldier) class hold all property in common, live communally like a military camp, and abolish private marriage and parenthood: 'breeding' festivals are rigged by the rulers under cover of a lottery to concentrate reproduction among the 'best' individuals, all children are removed at birth and raised collectively, and kinship terms (father, mother, brother, sister) are extended loosely by age-cohort to preserve social taboos without genetic tracking.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell treats this as Plato's attempt to eliminate private, possessive emotions that could compete with loyalty to the state, at the acknowledged cost of near-total state control over reproduction and family life.
core_concepts.historical_origin: An extension of the Spartan common-mess and shared-upbringing model, and Russell notes a parallel motive to that behind clerical celibacy.
examples: 'These women shall be, without exception, the common wives of these men, and no one shall have a wife of his own.'
Deformed children and children of inferior parents are to be 'put away in some mysterious unknown place.'
Mothers between twenty and forty, fathers between twenty-five and fifty-five, are the sanctioned reproductive ages; abortion or infanticide is compulsory outside them.
objections: Russell notes that if Plato's own kinship-avoidance rules (no father-daughter or mother-son unions, and generally no brother-sister unions) were followed strictly, they would in fact prohibit virtually all marriages, since almost anyone could plausibly be a 'sibling' under the loose age-based kinship system.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Echoed, per Russell, in the historical practice of clerical celibacy, which sought a similar reduction of private possessive attachment.

core_concepts.name: The 'noble lie' (myth of the metals)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Plato proposes that the rulers deliberately teach citizens a myth -- that God made some people of gold (fit to rule), some of silver (fit to be soldiers), and the rest of bronze and iron (fit for manual labor) -- to make the class system feel natural and God-given.
core_concepts.precise_definition: A government-sanctioned foundational myth (the 'one royal lie'), asserting citizens are born of different divinely ordained metals corresponding to their social class, intended to be believed by nearly the entire population (rulers possibly excepted) and sustained across generations through education.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It makes explicit that Plato's ideal state requires systematic falsehood administered by the state 'as a prerogative of the government, just as giving medicine is of physicians,' which Russell singles out as incompatible with the spirit of philosophy itself.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Presented by Plato as a deliberately constructed civic myth, not an inherited religious tradition.
examples: Russell compares its plausibility to the historically real Japanese doctrine that the Mikado descended from the sun-goddess, noting professors were dismissed for questioning it.
objections: Russell: 'Plato does not seem to realize that the compulsory acceptance of such myths is incompatible with philosophy, and involves a kind of education which stunts intelligence.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: The myth functions as a civic religion, deliberately engineered rather than organically inherited.

core_concepts.name: Plato's definition of justice
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Plato concludes that a society is 'just' when everyone does their own proper job and does not meddle in others' work -- traders trade, soldiers fight, guardians rule, and no one interferes with anyone else's role.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The Republic's culminating definition (reached in Book IV): justice consists in each class, and each individual, doing its own proper work without interference in the work of others, an idea Russell connects to an older Greek notion (traceable to Anaximander) of each thing having its 'appointed place and function,' violation of which constitutes hubris to be cosmically punished.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This definition permits, rather than forbids, inequalities of power and privilege, since inequality is only unjust, on Plato's view, if some non-guardian is actually wiser than some guardian -- a definition sharply at odds with modern, egalitarian conceptions of justice.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Traced by Russell to a pre-philosophical Greek religious/ethical intuition about cosmic order, evident already in Anaximander's fragment on things making 'reparation and satisfaction to one another for their injustice according to the appointed time.'
examples: Russell's analogy: no one thinks it unjust to put the best players on a football team, even though they gain thereby a great advantage.
objections: The definition presupposes a settled, traditional or ideologically fixed social order in which 'a man's job' can be determined; in Plato's own Republic, where no one has a legal father, this determination falls entirely to the state's judgment of aptitude, giving the state's purposes decisive power over what counts as legitimate work (e.g. Plato's condemnation of poetry as a 'job').
It is compatible with rule by an entrenched elite so long as no formal promotion/demotion rule is violated, regardless of whether that elite actually governs well or in the public interest.
competing_positions: The modern/democratic association of justice with equality, which Russell notes is quite foreign to Plato's usage.
Thrasymachus's view that 'justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Connects to a pre-philosophical religious sense of cosmic order and hubris found also in Heraclitus, Empedocles, and Parmenides.

core_concepts.name: Ethical objectivism vs. Thrasymachean relativism (the status of 'the Good')
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Is a claim like 'pleasure is good' actually true or false in the same way 'snow is white' is, or is 'good' just whatever the powerful decide it is, so that ethical disagreements are really just power struggles?
core_concepts.precise_definition: The debate, launched by Thrasymachus's claim that 'justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger,' over whether ethical statements have objective truth-value independent of desire and power, or whether, absent such objectivity, ethical disagreement reduces to contests of force or propaganda.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell treats this as one of the still-open questions in philosophy and uses it to explain why Plato's confident claim to know 'the Good' cannot simply be taken for granted -- it is itself among the most contested claims in his whole system.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Introduced dramatically via the character Thrasymachus (a real Sophist from Chalcedon) in Book I of the Republic.
examples: Russell's proposed practical test for ethical 'truth': whether virtually all investigators agree, as they do that 'water is composed of hydrogen and oxygen.'
The case of Galileo and of Christ's ethical innovations (e.g., 'it is wrong to hate your enemies') as examples of minority views later vindicated by something other than majority opinion or force.
objections: Socrates's rebuttal of Thrasymachus is, in Russell's judgment, done 'with quibbles' and 'never fairly faced.'
competing_positions: Plato's own confident ethical objectivism, which Russell says he holds 'without... being... aware of' the strength of Thrasymachus's challenge.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Remains, per Russell, 'one of the issues in philosophy that are still open.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Russell notes even theological answers (God determines the good) run into trouble, since calling God 'good' presupposes a standard of goodness independent of God's will.

arguments.title: Thrasymachus's claim that justice is the interest of the stronger
premises: In every state, the ruling power makes laws to its own advantage.
'Justice' is defined, in practice, as obedience to the laws.
Therefore what is called 'just' in any state is simply whatever serves the interest of whoever holds power there.
arguments.conclusion: Justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger.
arguments.explanation: Russell presents this as a serious challenge that Socrates never adequately answers within the dialogue, raising the broader question of whether 'good' and 'bad' have any meaning beyond what those with power (or, in ethics generally, whoever is speaking) desire.
objections: Socrates's response in the Republic, which Russell judges to consist of 'quibbles' rather than a genuine engagement with the underlying problem.
implications: If correct, ethical disputes -- including disputes about Plato's own Utopia -- 'can only be decided by emotional appeals, or by force,' since there would be no neutral standard of good and bad to appeal to.

arguments.title: Justice as each part doing its own job
premises: The best imaginable state has been constructed (the guardian/soldier/producer city).
One of the state's virtues, once identified, can be labeled 'justice.'
The city functions well when trader, soldier, and guardian each performs their own task without interfering in the others'.
arguments.conclusion: Justice, in both the state and (by analogy) the individual, consists in everyone (or every part of the soul) minding their own business and doing their own proper work.
arguments.explanation: Russell notes the nominal goal of the whole Republic was to define 'justice,' but the resulting definition is closer to what we would call 'not being a busybody' than to any modern sense involving equality or fairness; it also presupposes a fixed social order in which 'a man's job' can be determined, which fits a traditional or state-controlled society far better than a modern one of individual choice.
objections: The definition permits severe inequality of power and privilege as long as no formal boundary is transgressed, and does not by itself guarantee good or public-spirited government.
implications: Legitimizes rule by the guardian class as 'just' so long as the class structure (with its narrow provisions for promotion/demotion) is maintained.
Shows why Plato's 'justice' is compatible with, rather than opposed to, extreme political inequality.

key_distinctions: Guardians vs. soldiers/auxiliaries vs. common producers
'Music' (culture broadly) vs. 'gymnastics' (physical training) as the twin pillars of education
Plato's sense of 'justice' (everyone doing their own job) vs. the modern/democratic sense of justice as equality
Ethical objectivism (there is a fact of the matter about 'the Good') vs. Thrasymachean relativism (ethics reduces to the interest of the stronger)
An 'ideal' (impersonally, universally desired) vs. an ordinary personal desire, in Russell's own analysis of what ideals are
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell traces Plato's conception of justice back to Anaximander's pre-philosophical notion of cosmic justice and reparation for overstepping 'appointed' bounds, and situates it within a wider Greek outlook on fate and cosmic order found also in Heraclitus, Empedocles, and Parmenides. Plato's economic and educational proposals for the guardian class closely mirror the Spartan institutions detailed in the previous chapter.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell compares the guardian class to the Jesuits in colonial Paraguay, the ecclesiastical rulers of the Papal States before 1870, and the Communist Party of the U.S.S.R., and compares the communism of family to the historical practice of clerical celibacy. He also draws a direct line from the Thrasymachus/Socrates debate over ethical objectivity to Nietzsche's and modern totalitarian 'contests of power,' and notes that Christ's ethical innovations pose a similar challenge to any purely consensus-based theory of moral truth.
political_social_context: Plato imagined his Republic as potentially realizable, not merely as literary fantasy: many of its harshest-seeming provisions had real-world Spartan precedent, philosopher-rule had been attempted by Pythagoras, and Archytas the Pythagorean held real political influence in Taras during Plato's own lifetime. Plato's actual attempt to realize something like his ideal, by tutoring the younger Dionysius of Syracuse, failed; Russell notes that historical accident (Plato's connection to war-torn, commercial Syracuse rather than to a quieter colony) and the subsequent rise of Macedonia, which made 'all small States antiquated,' foreclosed any real chance of the Republic's establishment.
religion_science_culture_context: The 'noble lie' functions as a deliberately engineered civic religion; Plato's condemnation of Homer and Hesiod reshapes inherited religious literature to fit a state-directed moral pedagogy, while his banishment of dramatists reflects a broader suspicion of imitative and popular culture.
russell_presentation: Russell summarizes the Republic's structure (Utopia-building through Book V, the definition of 'philosopher' in Books VI-VII, and a survey of actual constitutions thereafter) before reconstructing the Utopia itself: the three classes and their fixed or exceptionally mobile roles; a censored, twofold ('music' and 'gymnastics') education aimed at producing gentlemanly courage and temperance; an austere communism of property for the guardians; a still more radical communism of women and children, complete with rigged eugenic 'lotteries,' compulsory abortion/infanticide outside sanctioned ages, and loosely extended kinship terms; and finally the 'noble lie' of the metals, meant to make the whole hierarchy seem divinely ordained. Russell treats these proposals with open irony and moral seriousness at once, repeatedly noting the gap between Plato's confident tone and the illiberal substance of his proposals. Turning to the Republic's official goal, the definition of justice, Russell shows that Plato's answer ('everyone doing his own job') is compatible with severe inequality and depends on a settled, state-determined sense of what a person's 'job' is. He then uses Thrasymachus's blunt challenge ('justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger') to open a genuinely unresolved philosophical question -- whether ethical claims are objectively true or merely expressions of desire and power -- arguing that Socrates never really answers Thrasymachus and that Plato is simply unaware of how strong the challenge is. Russell closes by noting that Plato likely intended the Republic to be actually founded, given real-world Spartan and Pythagorean precedents, and that its failure to be realized (via Dionysius of Syracuse) owed as much to historical accident as to its own defects.
critical_context: Later development: Russell's own extended digression on the nature of 'ideals' (as impersonally-desired-but-still-personally-rooted desires) is his original philosophical contribution appended to this chapter, not a claim about what Plato himself argued; it is offered as Russell's own attempt to frame the Thrasymachus debate rather than as Platonic doctrine, and readers should keep this Layer-3-adjacent digression distinct from Russell's report of Plato's actual text.
key_takeaways: Plato's Republic constructs the earliest Western Utopia: a three-class city (guardians, soldiers, producers) in which only guardians hold political power.
Guardian education combines rigidly censored 'music' (culture) with austere 'gymnastics' (physical training), banning most of Homer, Hesiod, and drama.
Guardians are to own no private property and to have no private families; reproduction is state-controlled via a rigged 'lottery' for eugenic ends, and children are raised communally.
The 'noble lie' (myth of gold/silver/bronze-iron natures) is meant to make the rigid class system seem divinely ordained, which Russell says is incompatible with philosophy itself.

Plato defines justice as everyone doing their own proper job without interference -- a definition compatible with severe inequality and quite different from the modern association of justice with equality.
Thrasymachus's claim that 'justice is the interest of the stronger' raises an unresolved philosophical question (objectivism vs. relativism in ethics) that Russell says Socrates never fairly answers.
study_notes:
It helps to read this chapter as Russell reading Plato on two tracks simultaneously: description and critique. On the descriptive track, build a clear picture of the mechanics -- who is in each class, how guardians are selected and educated, what 'communism' actually covers (property, then family), and what the noble lie is meant to accomplish. On the critical track, notice that Russell's objections are almost always structural rather than merely moralistic: he asks whether a proposal is internally consistent (e.g., pointing out that Plato's own kinship-avoidance rules, followed strictly, would prohibit nearly all marriage), and whether a definition does the work it claims to do (justice as 'doing one's own job' does not by itself rule out bad or self-interested rule, only rule that crosses formal class boundaries).

The Thrasymachus material is the philosophical high point of the chapter and deserves careful, slow reading. Russell is not simply reporting an ancient debate; he is using it to state, in his own voice, one of the deepest open problems in moral philosophy: is there objective truth in ethics comparable to objective truth in science, or does ethical language ultimately express desire, backed by power? Notice how Russell tests a 'consensus' theory of ethical truth against counterexamples like Galileo and Christ's ethical teaching, both of which were, at the time, minority views later vindicated by something other than majority agreement -- a challenge to any simple 'ethics is just what most people currently believe' position.

Finally, keep track of Russell's running analogy between Plato's guardians and later real institutions (the Society of Jesus in colonial Paraguay, the pre-1870 Papal States, the Soviet Communist Party): this is Russell inviting you to see the Republic not as a quaint historical curiosity but as a recurring political pattern.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The small ruling class in Plato's ideal city, chosen and trained to govern wisely.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The politically empowered class in Plato's Republic, selected initially by the legislator and mainly hereditary thereafter, subject to exceptional promotion or demotion, who alone exercise political authority and undergo the most demanding education.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A myth the government deliberately teaches, saying people are born of gold, silver, or bronze/iron, to justify the class system.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The 'one royal lie' Plato proposes the state inculcate, holding that God made guardians of gold, soldiers of silver, and producers of bronze and iron, intended to secure across-generation acceptance of the class hierarchy.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Plato's proposal that guardians share spouses and children in common rather than having private families.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Plato's proposal abolishing private marriage and parenthood among guardians, replacing it with state-arranged, eugenically manipulated mating festivals and communal child-rearing with no acknowledged biological parentage.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The claim that 'justice' really just means whatever benefits whoever is in power.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The position, voiced by the Sophist Thrasymachus in Republic Book I, that justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger, challenging any claim to an objective, power-independent standard of right and wrong.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Plato's final answer to 'what is justice?': everyone sticking to their own role and not meddling in others'.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Plato's Republic Book IV definition of justice as each class or individual performing its proper function without interference in others', tracing back to an older Greek notion of cosmic order and appointed place.

questions.prompt: What are the three classes in Plato's ideal city, and which alone holds political power?
questions.answer: The common people (producers), the soldiers (auxiliaries), and the guardians; only the guardians hold political power.
questions.explanation: This structure underlies nearly every other institution described in the chapter.

questions.prompt: What are the two components of Plato's proposed education, and roughly what does each cover?
questions.answer: 'Music,' covering the whole of culture (including censored poetry, drama, and musical modes), and 'gymnastics,' covering physical training and an austere dietary regimen.
questions.explanation: Plato's terms are broader than their modern English equivalents.

questions.prompt: Describe the 'noble lie' Plato proposes, and explain Russell's chief objection to it.
questions.answer: The myth that God made guardians of gold, soldiers of silver, and the common people of bronze and iron, meant to secure acceptance of the class system across generations; Russell objects that compulsory belief in such a myth is incompatible with philosophy and 'stunts intelligence.'
questions.explanation: Russell draws a comparison to the real historical Japanese myth of the Mikado's divine descent.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Thrasymachus's argument that justice is the interest of the stronger, and explain why Russell thinks Socrates fails to refute it.
questions.answer: Ruling powers make laws to serve their own interest; 'justice' in practice means obedience to those laws; therefore justice, wherever practiced, simply serves the interest of whoever rules. Russell argues Socrates responds only 'with quibbles' and never engages the deeper question of whether there is any objective standard of good and bad independent of power.
questions.explanation: This is presented as one of philosophy's still-open questions, not one Russell claims to resolve.

questions.prompt: Compare Plato's definition of justice with the modern, democratic association of justice with equality.
questions.answer: Plato's justice means each person or class doing its own proper work without interference, and is fully compatible with sharp inequalities of power and privilege as long as no one outside the guardian class is actually wiser than a guardian; the modern democratic sense, by contrast, closely links justice to equality, which Plato's definition does not require or even imply.
questions.explanation: Russell explicitly flags this as a major conceptual gap between ancient and modern usage.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, why might Plato's Republic have been intended as a realizable political program rather than pure fantasy?
questions.answer: Because many of its seemingly extreme provisions had real precedent at Sparta, philosopher-rule had already been attempted by Pythagoras, and Archytas the Pythagorean held genuine political influence in Taras during Plato's lifetime; Plato himself later tried, unsuccessfully, to realize something like it by tutoring the younger Dionysius of Syracuse.
questions.explanation: This context distinguishes the Republic from later Utopias that were written with no expectation of implementation.

questions.prompt: What problem does Russell find in Plato's rules against incestuous unions under the communism of women and children?
questions.answer: Because everyone of the right age is addressed as 'father,' 'mother,' 'brother,' or 'sister,' Plato's ban on parent-child unions and general (though not absolute) ban on sibling unions, if followed strictly and consistently, would end up prohibiting virtually all marriages, since almost any potential partner could plausibly count as a sibling.
questions.explanation: Russell treats this as evidence that Plato had not fully thought through the implications of the scheme.

flashcards.front: What are the three classes in Plato's Utopia?
flashcards.back: Guardians (rulers), soldiers/auxiliaries, and the common people (producers).

flashcards.front: What two things make up Plato's system of education?
flashcards.back: 'Music' (culture broadly, including literature and the arts) and 'gymnastics' (physical training).

flashcards.front: Which two musical modes does Plato permit, and for what reasons?
flashcards.back: The Dorian (for courage) and the Phrygian (for temperance); the Lydian (sorrow) and Ionian (relaxation) are banned.

flashcards.front: What happens to dramatists in Plato's ideal city?
flashcards.back: They are ceremonially honored, then banished, since imitating villains, women, or inferiors is deemed unfit for good men.

flashcards.front: What economic arrangement applies to guardians?
flashcards.back: Communism of property: no private wealth beyond bare necessities, communal living and dining like a military camp.

flashcards.front: What is Plato's proposal for guardian family life?

flashcards.front: What is the 'noble lie' or myth of the metals?
flashcards.back: A state-taught myth that guardians are made of gold, soldiers of silver, and the common people of bronze and iron, meant to make the class hierarchy seem divinely ordained.

flashcards.front: What real-world myth does Russell compare to Plato's noble lie?
flashcards.back: The Japanese myth that the Mikado descended from the sun-goddess.

flashcards.front: How does Plato ultimately define 'justice' in the Republic?
flashcards.back: Everyone (and every class) doing their own proper job without interfering in others' work.

flashcards.front: Who challenges Socrates with the claim that 'justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger'?

flashcards.back: The younger Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse; the attempt failed, as the young man 'turned out disappointingly' (a point made fully in the following chapter, though the failed venture itself is noted here).

flashcards.back: The Jesuits in colonial Paraguay, the ecclesiastics of the Papal States before 1870, and the Communist Party of the U.S.S.R.

quiz.prompt: How many classes make up Plato's ideal city?
quiz.explanation: Common people, soldiers, and guardians -- only the last holds political power.

quiz.prompt: Which two musical modes does Plato allow in his ideal city?
quiz.explanation: Dorian promotes courage and Phrygian promotes temperance, per the chapter.

quiz.explanation: Guardians are to have 'no private property beyond what is absolutely necessary,' and gold and silver are forbidden entirely.

quiz.prompt: What is the purpose of the 'noble lie' (myth of gold, silver, and bronze/iron natures)?
options: To justify going to war with Sparta
To make the class hierarchy seem divinely ordained and thus stable across generations
To explain the origin of the universe
To excuse the guardians from military service
quiz.explanation: The myth is meant to secure belief in, and thus stability of, the class structure.

quiz.prompt: Plato ultimately defines 'justice' as everyone doing their own ___ without interfering in others'.
quiz.explanation: This is the Republic's Book IV definition, reached after constructing the ideal city.

quiz.prompt: Who claims in Book I of the Republic that 'justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger'?
quiz.explanation: Thrasymachus, a Sophist from Chalcedon, voices this challenge.

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, what problem arises from Plato's rules against incestuous unions under communism of women and children?
options: They are too permissive and allow all unions
Strictly applied, they would prohibit virtually all marriages given the loose kinship-by-age system
